boundary_rationale: Opens at the book’s absolute incipit with a bare, unheaded father-son succession — אָדָ֥ם שֵׁ֖ת אֱנֽוֹשׁ (“Adam, Seth, Enosh,” WEB v.1) — naming exactly one heir per generation, with no “sons of” formula anywhere in the run. It closes at v.4 because the chain there fans from a single name to Noah’s three sons at once, נֹ֥חַ שֵׁ֖ם חָ֥ם וָיָֽפֶת (“Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth,” WEB), and v.5 answers immediately with the register-head formula בְּנֵ֣י יֶ֔פֶת (“The sons of Japheth,” WEB) that structures the rest of the survey through v.23 — a form neither v.1 nor any verse before v.5 uses. The single-witness samekh following v.4 corroborates this seam only weakly, never driving it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit past v.4 into the Table of Nations loses because the strict one-heir-per-generation succession of vv.1-4 never recurs once the branching “sons of X” formula begins at v.5.

boundary_rationale: The register head בְּנֵ֣י יֶ֔פֶת (“The sons of Japheth,” WEB v.5) opens a construct-plural benei-X head tier that recurs at בְּנֵ֖י חָ֑ם (v.8, “The sons of Ham”), וּבְנֵ֣י כ֔וּשׁ (v.9, “The sons of Cush”), and בְּנֵ֣י שֵׁ֔ם (v.17, “The sons of Shem”) — but that head-tier alone accounts for only six of the span's nineteen verses (5,6,7,8,9,17). From v.10 the Ham line switches to a finite begetting clause, וְכ֖וּשׁ יָלַ֣ד אֶת נִמְר֑וֹד ה֣וּא הֵחֵ֔ל לִהְי֥וֹת גִּבּ֖וֹר בָּאָֽרֶץ (“Cush became the father of Nimrod,” WEB), and the Shem line switches identically at v.18, וְאַרְפַּכְשַׁ֖ד יָלַ֣ד אֶת שָׁ֑לַח וְשֶׁ֖לַח יָלַ֥ד אֶת עֵֽבֶר (“Arpachshad became the father of Shelah,” WEB); vv.12,14-16,21-22 continue those same clauses by waw-plus-accusative-particle rather than by any register head. Both switches read as elaboration nested under the branch each already stood inside — v.10 continues Cush, already named by v.8's Ham-head and re-headed at v.9; v.18 continues Arpachshad, already named by v.17's Shem-head — not as fresh register heads, since neither verse restarts the benei-X formula and the begetting-clause device never launches an independent branch anywhere else in this table. The unit closes on כָּל אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י יָקְטָֽן (v.23, “All these were the sons of Joktan,” WEB), a construct closure binding to Joktan alone, four generations under Shem. On its face that formula shuts only the Shem sub-branch; but it is also the sole closing formula the whole three-branch table receives anywhere in vv.5-23, since neither Japheth's branch (vv.5-7) nor Ham's (vv.8-16) ends with a ‘these are’ formula of its own. Read against that asymmetry, the Joktan closure is the table's only available shut-point and is taken to discharge the whole register by elimination rather than by lexical reach. The seam at v.24 is unmistakable: שֵׁ֥ם אַרְפַּכְשַׁ֖ד שָֽׁלַח drops back to the bare chain-form last used in vv.1-4, abandoning both the benei-X head and the begetting-clause devices that had governed vv.5-23 together.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the survey into three rows at each ‘sons of X’ head (Japheth v.5, Ham v.8, Shem v.17) loses because the table receives exactly one closing formula in nineteen verses, at v.23, and a three-way split would leave two of the three resulting rows with no textual marker for their own end.

boundary_rationale: After the Table of Nations shuts at v.23, שֵׁ֥ם אַרְפַּכְשַׁ֖ד שָֽׁלַח (“Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah,” WEB v.24) reopens the bare succession-chain form last seen in v.4, resuming — not repeating — the Shem line already surveyed in branching form at בְּנֵ֣י שֵׁ֔ם (“The sons of Shem,” WEB v.17), but now stripped to the single-heir device that carried Adam to Noah. It runs to אַבְרָ֖ם ה֥וּא אַבְרָהָֽם (“Abram (also called Abraham),” WEB v.27) and stops there, one verse short of naming Abraham’s own sons, because v.28 answers with its own fresh register head, בְּנֵי֙ אַבְרָהָ֔ם (“The sons of Abraham,” WEB), switching form again.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading vv.24-27 as a coda to the Shem branch of the Table of Nations loses because the form is not a continuation of v.17’s “sons of X” idiom but a deliberate reversion to the pre-flood chain’s bare-name style, marking a fresh unit rather than an appendix.

boundary_rationale: The head בְּנֵי֙ אַבְרָהָ֔ם יִצְחָ֖ק וְיִשְׁמָעֵֽאל (“The sons of Abraham,” WEB v.28) names only Isaac and Ishmael. The very next verse nests its own toledot head under that announcement, אֵ֖לֶּה תֹּלְדוֹתָ֑ם (“These are their generations,” WEB v.29) — the chapter's only occurrence of that noun and one of just six genuine elleh-type demonstratives in ch.1 (vv.23,29,31,33,43,54; the similarly spelled word at v.52 is the personal name Elah, not a demonstrative) — which opens the Ishmael roster and closes it at אֵ֥לֶּה הֵ֖ם בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׁמָעֵֽאל (v.31, “these are the sons of Ishmael,” WEB). Keturah, by contrast, is introduced only afterward, as Abraham's concubine rather than as a party to v.28's own announcement: וּבְנֵ֨י קְטוּרָ֜ה פִּילֶ֣גֶשׁ אַבְרָהָ֗ם (v.32, “The sons of Keturah, Abraham’s concubine,” WEB), a vav-prefixed register head matching the subordinate-branch pattern this chapter uses for satellite lines elsewhere — וּבְנֵ֖י גֹּ֑מֶר (Gomer, v.6) and וּבְנֵ֥י יָוָ֖ן (Javan, v.7) both nested under Japheth's asyndetic v.5 head, וּבְנֵ֣י כ֔וּשׁ (Cush, v.9) nested under Ham's asyndetic v.8 head — rather than a second primary heading standing beside v.28. Not every conjunctive benei-head in the chapter fits that satellite pattern, however: וּבְנֵ֣י שֵׂעִ֔יר (v.38, the sons of Seir, WEB) carries the identical vav-prefixed morphology yet cannot be read as a satellite of Esau's own asyndetic head, since Seir is absent from the five sons of Esau named at v.35 (אֱלִיפַ֛ז רְעוּאֵ֥ל וִיע֖וּשׁ וְיַעְלָ֥ם וְקֹֽרַח); decision M8-1Chr-006 already treats 1:38 on that basis, so the vav-prefix alone is not offered here as a reliable subordination marker. Keturah's own roster closes at כָּל אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י קְטוּרָֽה (v.33, “all these were the sons of Keturah,” WEB). The unit ends there because v.34 pivots to a narrative-verb clause, וַיּ֥וֹלֶד אַבְרָהָ֖ם אֶת יִצְחָ֑ק (“Abraham became the father of Isaac,” WEB), finally taking up the Isaac line v.28 deferred and launching the Esau/Israel split — a different formal device from either the toledot head or the vav-prefixed subordinate head that governed the row up to this point.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Ishmael (29-31) from Keturah (32-33) into separate rows loses because the two sub-heads sit at different structural depths — v.29's toledot head directly discharges v.28's own announcement, while v.32's vav-prefixed head introduces a party v.28 never names — and both close before v.34 resumes the elect line, so splitting the row would cut a two-level structure the text itself keeps under one v.28 frame.

boundary_rationale: v.34 does double duty: וַיּ֥וֹלֶד אַבְרָהָ֖ם אֶת יִצְחָ֑ק בְּנֵ֣י יִצְחָ֔ק עֵשָׂ֖ו וְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל (“Abraham became the father of Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel,” WEB) both completes the long-deferred Isaac notice from v.28 and supplies the register head for what follows — Israel deferred to ch.2, Esau elaborated at once. Because the verse cannot be split, the row is anchored to what it introduces rather than to the Ishmael/Keturah row above. The verse carries a double samekh (SAMEKH+SAMEKH, single-witness), a weak corroboration of a pivot the bifurcation formula itself already requires. בְּנֵ֖י עֵשָׂ֑ו (“The sons of Esau,” WEB v.35) heads the elaboration proper, with grandsons nested under it at בְּנֵ֖י אֱלִיפָ֑ז (“The sons of Eliphaz,” WEB v.36) and בְּנֵ֖י רְעוּאֵ֑ל (“The sons of Reuel,” WEB v.37). The row closes before v.38, whose head וּבְנֵ֣י שֵׂעִ֔יר (“The sons of Seir,” WEB) names an eponym not counted among Esau’s own sons in vv.35-37.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching v.34 to the preceding Ishmael/Keturah row loses because the verse’s own second clause is the register head that structures vv.35-37, not merely a close to what precedes.

boundary_rationale: וּבְנֵ֣י שֵׂעִ֔יר (v.38, “The sons of Seir,” WEB) opens on the register's own benei-X tier, but the diagnostic is not morphological — v.35's בְּנֵ֖י עֵשָׂ֑ו is asyndetic while v.38 carries a conjunctive waw — the diagnostic is that Seir himself is absent from the five sons of Esau v.35 names (אֱלִיפַ֛ז רְעוּאֵ֥ל וִיע֖וּשׁ וְיַעְלָ֥ם וְקֹֽרַח), so v.38 introduces a genuinely new, unrelated eponym rather than continuing Esau's own line. From there the verse launches a run that expands Seir's seven named sons in turn: Lotan's own sons at וּבְנֵ֥י לוֹטָ֖ן חֹרִ֣י (v.39), Shobal's and Zibeon's at v.40 (בְּנֵ֣י שׁוֹבָ֔ל עַלְיָ֧ן וּמָנַ֛חַת וְעֵיבָ֖ל שְׁפִ֣י), then Anah's son and Dishon's sons at v.41 (בְּנֵ֥י עֲנָ֖ה דִּישׁ֑וֹן וּבְנֵ֣י דִישׁ֔וֹן חַמְרָ֥ן וְאֶשְׁבָּ֖ן וְיִתְרָ֥ן וּכְרָֽן), and Ezer's and Dishon's at v.42 (בְּֽנֵי אֵ֔צֶר בִּלְהָ֥ן וְזַעֲוָ֖ן יַעֲקָ֑ן בְּנֵ֥י דִישׁ֖וֹן ע֥וּץ וַאֲרָֽן), with no closing 'these are' formula anywhere in the run — a real formal gap, not filled by the double samekh after v.41, since that mark falls mid-run over a sub-list rather than at a register edge. The v.42 closing clause names דִישׁ֖וֹן plene with vav — the identical spelling given to Anah's son at v.41 — not the pointed form וְדִישָֽׁן used for Seir's own seventh son at v.38; WEB's 'sons of Dishan' at v.42 disambiguates the English from v.41's 'Dishon' but is a translator's gloss rather than a distinct Hebrew name, so the row's account of the run as covering Seir's seven sons in turn rests on WEB's differentiated naming rather than on the MT spelling alone, which repeats v.41's form. The row ends because v.43 opens an entirely different register, וְאֵ֣לֶּה הַמְּלָכִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר מָלְכוּ֙ בְּאֶ֣רֶץ אֱד֔וֹם (“Now these are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom,” WEB), naming kings rather than sons and adding a historical synchronism absent from every preceding line in the chapter. Marks across this row are disclosed as tier-3, single-witness, non-driving throughout: samekh follows v.39 and v.40, a doubled samekh follows v.41 (doubling disclosed), and a pe follows v.42 at the row's own closing edge; none of the four corroborates or counts against the boundary on its own.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v.41's double samekh (into 38-40 and 41-42) loses because vv.39-42 are one unbroken expansion of the seven sons named in v.38, and the mark tracks list-item granularity within that expansion, not a literary seam.

boundary_rationale: The register opens on its own historical footing, not merely a fresh “sons of X” head: וְאֵ֣לֶּה הַמְּלָכִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר מָלְכוּ֙ בְּאֶ֣רֶץ אֱד֔וֹם לִפְנֵ֥י מְלָךְ מֶ֖לֶךְ לִבְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל (“Now these are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel,” WEB v.43) supplies a synchronism no earlier line in the chapter carries. From v.44 the text runs a fixed death-succession refrain, וַיָּ֖מָת בָּ֑לַע וַיִּמְלֹ֣ךְ תַּחְתָּ֔יו (“Bela died, and ... reigned in his place,” WEB), repeated down the king-list to its final entry, Hadad’s, which alone names the lineage of his wife across three generations, וְשֵׁ֨ם אִשְׁתּ֤וֹ מְהֵיטַבְאֵל֙ בַּת מַטְרֵ֔ד בַּ֖ת מֵ֥י זָהָֽב (“His wife’s name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab,” WEB v.50). The refrain then breaks at v.51: Hadad dies again, but no “reigned in his place” clause follows — instead וַיָּ֖מָת הֲדָ֑ד וַיִּהְיוּ֙ אַלּוּפֵ֣י אֱד֔וֹם (“Then Hadad died. The chiefs of Edom were,” WEB) opens a title-list — so the succession chain’s actual close is v.50, and the chiefs’ material belongs to the next row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the kings row through v.51 (since “Then Hadad died” echoes the death-formula) loses because the clause that always follows a king’s death elsewhere in this list — “reigned in his place” — is absent there, replaced by the chiefs’ own register head and its first name.

boundary_rationale: v.51 opens by echoing the verb that closed each king's entry, but its full clause pivots at once from death-notice into a title-and-count register that runs through the rest of the row: וַיָּ֖מָת הֲדָ֑ד (“Then Hadad died,” WEB) is followed in the same verse by three chiefs, not one — וַיִּהְיוּ֙ אַלּוּפֵ֣י אֱד֔וֹם אַלּ֥וּף תִּמְנָ֛ע אַלּ֥וּף עליה עַֽלְוָ֖ה אַלּ֥וּף יְתֵֽת (“chief Timna, chief Aliah, chief Jetheth,” WEB v.51), the second name carrying both a ketiv and its qere together in the source, which WEB's 'Aliah' follows on the ketiv consonants. Since the verse cannot be split, and its own three-chief count matches vv.52-53 exactly (אַלּ֧וּף אָהֳלִיבָמָ֛ה אַלּ֥וּף אֵלָ֖ה אַלּ֥וּף פִּינֹֽן, v.52; אַלּ֥וּף קְנַ֛ז אַלּ֥וּף תֵּימָ֖ן אַלּ֣וּף מִבְצָֽר, v.53), it belongs with the chiefs, not the kings. v.54 breaks that three-per-verse count rather than extending it — אַלּ֥וּף מַגְדִּיאֵ֖ל אַלּ֣וּף עִירָ֑ם names only two chiefs before the chapter's own explicit tally, אֵ֖לֶּה אַלּוּפֵ֥י אֱדֽוֹם (“These are the chiefs of Edom,” WEB v.54), the last of the chapter's several closure formulas and the row's own close. A samekh follows 1:51 (single-witness), a weak signal toward the v.51|v.52 seam this row rejects, and a pe follows 1:54 (single-witness), weak corroboration of the row's own close; neither tier-3 mark outweighs the tier-1 case already made from the three-per-verse chief count and the register head inside v.51.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping v.51 with the kings' chain and opening the chiefs row at v.52 loses because v.51's own content — the chiefs' register head and first three names — already belongs formally to the three-per-verse chieftain pattern that runs unbroken through vv.52-53, with v.54 closing the row on two names plus its own summary formula rather than a fourth triplet.

boundary_rationale: The unit opens with a national headline formula, אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י (v.1; WEB 'These are the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun,'). What licenses this as an opening is not the formula's own identity -- a book-wide sweep of the elleh(+hayu)+benei construction returns 23 occurrences, and most of them, including the book's own anaphoric exemplar at 2:33 (אֵ֥לֶּה הָי֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י יְרַחְמְאֵֽל) and ch.1's own כָּל אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י יָקְטָֽן at 1:23, stand AFTER the names they gather, closing a list rather than opening one -- but its verse-initial position at 2:1 together with the twelve tribal names that follow inside the same verse. It runs the twelve-tribe roll to its own natural stop at 2:2's final pair, גָּ֥ד וְאָשֵֽׁר (v.2; WEB 'Gad, and Asher.'), a bare enumeration with no further names to gather. The seam is decisive at 2:3 because the head there narrows to one tribe, בְּנֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֗ה (v.3; WEB 'The sons of Judah:'), starting a Judah-specific genealogy rather than continuing the national list. A samekh follows 2:2 (single-witness), weak corroboration of the same break the wording already makes.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 2:1-4 as a single 'introduction to Judah' unit loses because 2:1-2 names all twelve sons of Israel, functioning as the header for the whole multi-chapter tribal register (chs 2-8), not as a Judah preface.

boundary_rationale: Having narrowed from the national list, the text opens Judah's own register, בְּנֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֗ה עֵ֤ר וְאוֹנָן֙ וְשֵׁלָ֔ה (oshb:1Chr.2.3; WEB 'The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, and Shelah'), then folds in a short narrative aside on Er's death, רַ֛ע בְּעֵינֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה וַיְמִיתֵֽהוּ (oshb:1Chr.2.3; WEB '...was wicked in Yahweh's sight; and he killed him.'), before Tamar's sons are added and the generation is tallied shut: כָּל בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה חֲמִשָּֽׁה (oshb:1Chr.2.4; WEB 'All the sons of Judah were five.'). That count formula is a self-contained closure of the type this book uses elsewhere to shut a generation (cf. the parallel five-count at 2:6), so the unit ends there rather than running on. 2:5 reopens with a narrower head, בְּנֵי פֶ֖רֶץ (oshb:1Chr.2.5; WEB 'The sons of Perez:'), confirming the seam: a fresh subject is marked before the next generation is treated. A samekh follows 2:4 (single-witness), weakly corroborating a break the count formula already secures; samekh also follow several verses in this immediate stretch (single-witness), a WLC list-item density this row does not chase.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through 2:8 to swallow the Perez/Zerah branches loses because 2:4's explicit five-count closes Judah's own generation on its own terms, with no warrant to override a stated tally for a later, unmarked stopping point.

boundary_rationale: This row gathers Judah's two grandsons' branches before the text swings to Hezron's own dynasty. It opens where Judah's generation left off, בְּנֵי פֶ֖רֶץ חֶצְר֥וֹן וְחָמֽוּל (v.5; WEB 'The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul.'), then pivots at once to the sibling branch, וּבְנֵ֣י זֶ֗רַח (v.6; WEB 'The sons of Zerah:'), which is itself tallied, כֻּלָּ֥ם חֲמִשָּֽׁה (v.6; WEB '...five of them in all.'). That tally closes Zerah's own five sons, not the row's governing frame -- unlike the preceding row's own closing tally at 2:4, כָּל בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה חֲמִשָּֽׁה ('all the sons of Judah were five'), which totals Judah's whole generation and ends that row outright -- and is followed, with no register restart, by two further single-name notices whose generational depth is not parallel: v.8's Ethan continues a name already listed among Zerah's five sons at v.6, one generation down, while v.7's Carmi has no antecedent anywhere in ch.2 and opens cold -- וּבְנֵ֖י כַּרְמִ֑י עָכָר֙ עוֹכֵ֣ר יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר מָעַ֖ל בַּחֵֽרֶם (v.7; WEB 'The son of Carmi: Achar, the troubler of Israel, who committed a trespass in the devoted thing.') and וּבְנֵ֥י אֵיתָ֖ן עֲזַרְיָֽה (v.8; WEB 'The son of Ethan: Azariah.'). The case for holding 2:7-2:8 together rests instead on their shared formal shape -- both plural construct benei heads carrying a single following name, the same shape as v.5's own opening, with 'The son of' a WEB translation choice rather than a change in the underlying Hebrew form -- not on parallel descent. Since v.8 carries no tally of its own and is unquestionably still part of this table, an internal tally cannot be what ends a row here; v.6's tally is sub-branch bookkeeping of the same kind that never closes anything at v.8, and the row instead runs on to the point where the text changes device altogether. That change comes at 2:9, whose relative clause and accusative-marked member list are absent from all three preceding heads: וּבְנֵ֥י חֶצְר֖וֹן אֲשֶׁ֣ר נוֹלַד ל֑וֹ אֶת יְרַחְמְאֵ֥ל וְאֶת רָ֖ם וְאֶת כְּלוּבָֽי (v.9; WEB 'The sons also of Hezron, who were born to him: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai.') -- the relative clause אֲשֶׁ֣ר נוֹלַד ל֑וֹ and the et-marked triad, not WEB's supplied 'also' (which renders the same waw that opens vv.6-8 and carries no MT counterpart of its own), are the actual formal break, resuming Hezron by name after the row's own excursus through Zerah, Carmi, and Ethan. Samekh follow 2:5, 2:6, and 2:7 (single-witness), a dense list-item pattern tracking the sub-heads inside this table without dictating where the table itself ends.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The stronger rival is not splitting every sub-head but ending the row at 2:6, where Zerah's own five-son tally falls, and reading 2:7-8 as a separate Carmi/Ethan coda; that reading loses because 2:8 carries the identical bare benei-plus-single-name shape as 2:7 with no tally or closure marking a fresh start between them, so a break at 2:6 would sever a two-verse unit that shares one form and has no internal seam of its own.

boundary_rationale: The row opens on the resumptive three-son head, וּבְנֵ֥י חֶצְר֖וֹן אֲשֶׁ֣ר נוֹלַד ל֑וֹ אֶת יְרַחְמְאֵ֥ל וְאֶת רָ֖ם וְאֶת כְּלוּבָֽי (v.9; WEB 'The sons also of Hezron, who were born to him: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai.'), and the very next verse unpacks the middle-named son at once, וְרָ֖ם הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת עַמִּינָדָ֑ב (v.10; WEB 'Ram became the father of Amminadab'), the first of a waw+name+holid chain that recurs at 2:11,12,13 inside this same span and thirteen times across the whole chapter. The chain runs in that idiom down to David's own generation, closing its count at אֹ֚צֶם הַשִּׁשִּׁ֔י דָּוִ֖יד הַשְּׁבִעִֽי (v.15; WEB 'Ozem the sixth, and David the seventh'), then adds a sibling note, וְאַחְיוֹתֵיהֶ֖ם צְרוּיָ֣ה וַאֲבִיגָ֑יִל (v.16, qere; ketiv ואחיתיהם; WEB '...and their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail'), ending on Amasa's father, יֶ֖תֶר הַיִּשְׁמְעֵאלִֽי (v.17; WEB 'Jether the Ishmaelite.'). The unit closes at 2:18 not because that verse abandons the chain's own verb shape — וְכָלֵ֣ב בֶּן חֶצְר֗וֹן הוֹלִ֛יד (v.18; WEB 'Caleb the son of Hezron became the father of') reproduces the identical waw+PN+holid opening used at 2:10-13 — but because it re-anchors that verb to Hezron by patronym, בֶּן חֶצְר֗וֹן, after nine verses in which the chain had travelled away from him through Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salma, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, and David. That re-anchoring, not a change of formal device, is what marks the seam: the row's own line has moved on from Hezron entirely by 2:15-17, and 2:18 explicitly returns to him by name before opening a new branch. No pe or samekh falls anywhere across 2:9-2:17; that silence is not weighed against the boundary, since mark absence is never evidence either way here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at 2:10, where the 'became the father of' verb first appears, loses because 2:9's three-son head is the antecedent the chain immediately unpacks — head and chain form one resumptive move, not two.

boundary_rationale: The row opens with Caleb's own head, וְכָלֵ֣ב בֶּן חֶצְר֗וֹן הוֹלִ֛יד (v.18; WEB 'Caleb the son of Hezron became the father of'), which runs through his wives' sons to the craftsman line ending וְחוּר֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת אוּרִ֔י וְאוּרִ֖י הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת בְּצַלְאֵֽל (v.20; WEB 'Hur became the father of Uri, and Uri became the father of Bezalel.'). The subject then swings back to Hezron himself, not by a wayyiqtol resumption but by a fronted temporal adverb plus a bare 3ms qatal with postposed subject, וְאַחַ֗ר בָּ֤א חֶצְרוֹן֙ (v.21; WEB 'Afterward Hezron went in to'), a construction distinct from the row's own genuine wayyiqtols at וַתָּ֖מָת עֲזוּבָ֑ה (v.19) and, later, וַיִּקַּ֣ח גְּשֽׁוּר (v.23). The same we-ahar adverb recurs exactly once more in the whole book, three verses later at וְאַחַ֥ר מוֹת חֶצְר֖וֹן (v.24; WEB 'After Hezron died'), though not in an identical construction: v.21's adverb governs a finite 3ms qatal (בָּ֤א) with Hezron as postposed subject, while v.24's adverb governs the construct מוֹת ('the dying of') with חֶצְר֖וֹן as its genitive, not a finite verb; v.24's own finite verb is the wayyiqtol וַתֵּ֣לֶד, whose subject is וְאֵ֤שֶׁת חֶצְרוֹן֙ אֲבִיָּ֔ה. It is this shared we-ahar adverb alone, not an identical device, that the pairing argument for holding 2:21-24 together now rests on: so 2:21 and 2:24 form a matched pair of appendices rather than an isolated aside: both resume Hezron by the same rare device, both add a further marriage-and-offspring notice, and neither restarts with a 'sons of X' register head or closes with a summary formula of the kind that elsewhere in this chapter marks a fresh unit. Read as a pair, the device argues for keeping 2:21-24 together as two linked continuations of Hezron's own story rather than for splitting either one out alone: it stays grammatically Hezron's material, shifting only from Caleb's descendants to Hezron's own further offspring, before the row closes on his death and posthumous son, וַתֵּ֣לֶד ל֔וֹ אֶת אַשְׁח֖וּר אֲבִ֥י תְקֽוֹעַ (v.24; WEB '...Abijah, Hezron’s wife, bore him Ashhur the father of Tekoa.'). This join must confront 2:23's own kol-elleh-benei closure, כָּל אֵ֕לֶּה בְּנֵ֖י מָכִ֥יר אֲבִי גִלְעָֽד ('all these were the sons of Machir the father of Gilead'), the only such tier-1 closure formula inside this row's 2:18-2:24 span and the same anaphoric class decision M8-1Chr-002 treats as strong enough to shut a whole register at 1:23. That formula closes only the Machir/Jair excursus (2:21-22), not the row's whole Hezron block: what keeps 2:24 attached across it is the we-ahar device just described, which resumes Hezron himself rather than continuing the Machir/Jair material the 2:23 formula has already sealed. The seam to 2:25 is the genuine tier-1 break: וַיִּהְי֧וּ בְנֵי יְרַחְמְאֵ֛ל בְּכ֥וֹר חֶצְר֖וֹן הַבְּכ֣וֹר רָ֑ם וּבוּנָ֥ה וָאֹ֛רֶן וָאֹ֖צֶם אֲחִיָּֽה (v.25; WEB 'The sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron were Ram the firstborn'), a full patronym-plus-firstborn head opening the next son's line, a device 2:21 and 2:24 both lack. A samekh follows 2:20 (single-witness), sitting right at the internal turn between Caleb's craftsmen and Hezron's late marriage — weak corroboration that a sub-shift is felt there, even though this row treats both halves as one Hezron-generation cluster rather than splitting on it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at 2:21 on participant-change grounds loses because the fronted ahar-plus-qatal that reopens Hezron there is the same rare device that reopens him again at 2:24 with no register-head or summary formula at either point, so treating the first occurrence as unit-ending but not the second would split a matched appendix pair on an inconsistent standard rather than on a textual seam.

boundary_rationale: The unit opens on the full patronym-and-rank head, וַיִּהְי֧וּ בְנֵי יְרַחְמְאֵ֛ל בְּכ֥וֹר חֶצְר֖וֹן הַבְּכ֣וֹר רָ֑ם וּבוּנָ֥ה וָאֹ֛רֶן וָאֹ֖צֶם אֲחִיָּֽה (v.25; WEB 'The sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron were Ram the firstborn'), but the identical shape recurs twice more inside the span it opens: וַיִּהְי֥וּ בְנֵי רָ֖ם בְּכ֣וֹר יְרַחְמְאֵ֑ל מַ֥עַץ וְיָמִ֖ין וָעֵֽקֶר (v.27; WEB 'The sons of Ram the firstborn of Jerahmeel were Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.'), which even keeps the same bekhor-rank element, and וַיִּהְי֥וּ בְנֵי אוֹנָ֖ם שַׁמַּ֣י וְיָדָ֑ע (v.28; WEB 'The sons of Onam were Shammai and Jada'). A book-wide sweep for this exact verse-initial construction returns six occurrences, three of them — 2:25, 2:27, and 2:28 — inside this one span; both internal recurrences name figures already introduced in 2:25-26 (Ram and Onam are Jerahmeel's and his second wife's own sons), so they read as subordinate sub-heads carried under the 2:25 frame rather than as independent register openings, but the opening edge is accordingly a signal that fires three times inside its own unit, not once. The span holds together through a second-wife notice (2:26) and these two further branch generations (2:27-32), closing on אֵ֥לֶּה הָי֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י יְרַחְמְאֵֽל (v.33; WEB 'These were the sons of Jerahmeel.'). That closure is positional rather than a shared formula with this chapter's own neighbors: it stands verse-final, gathering the antecedent names already given, whereas the superficially similar strings at 2:1 (אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י) and 2:50 (אֵ֤לֶּה הָיוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י) both stand at word 0 with their lists following — opposite discourse functions dressed in the same words, so 2:33 is the strongest available signal on its own positional grounds, not because it echoes an opening device used elsewhere. The next verse breaks the pattern entirely: וְלֹֽא הָיָ֧ה לְשֵׁשָׁ֛ן בָּנִ֖ים כִּ֣י אִם בָּנ֑וֹת (v.34; WEB 'Now Sheshan had no sons, but only daughters.'), a negated-existence clause opening a new move rather than continuing the closed Jerahmeel tally. Samekh follow 2:26, 2:30, and 2:32 inside this stretch (single-witness) — dense sub-list marking this row does not let override the governing summary closure, which itself carries no mark at all; that mark's absence is not weighed against it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at either internal recurrence — 2:27, where Ram's branch takes over, or 2:28, where Onam's does — loses because both figures are Jerahmeel's own descendants already introduced in 2:25-26, so both sub-heads are subordinate developments gathered under the single 2:33 closure rather than independent register openings with their own compass.

boundary_rationale: This row is opened by the exception clause וְלֹֽא הָיָ֧ה לְשֵׁשָׁ֛ן בָּנִ֖ים כִּ֣י אִם בָּנ֑וֹת (oshb:1Chr.2.34; WEB 'Now Sheshan had no sons, but only daughters.'), which pulls a figure already named inside the closed 2:25-33 unit (Sheshan appears at 2:31) back out for individual treatment — a distinct move, not a continuation of that closed tally. It runs through the marriage to the Egyptian servant Jarha and a long 'became the father of' chain, closing on Elishama, וְשַׁלּוּם֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת יְקַמְיָ֔ה וִֽיקַמְיָ֖ה הֹלִ֥יד אֶת אֱלִישָׁמָֽע (oshb:1Chr.2.41; WEB '...and Shallum became the father of Jekamiah, and Jekamiah became the father of Elishama.'). The chain simply stops — no summary formula ends it — but 2:42 reopens decisively with a fresh, differently-labeled Caleb head, וּבְנֵ֤י כָלֵב֙ אֲחִ֣י יְרַחְמְאֵ֔ל (oshb:1Chr.2.42; WEB 'The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel were'), naming Caleb by his relation to Jerahmeel rather than continuing Sheshan's line, the tier-1 marker this row's close relies on. No pe or samekh falls between 2:34 and 2:41 in this list, so the boundary rests on the wording alone, the mark's silence weighed as nothing either way.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this material back into the 2:25-33 unit because Sheshan is already named there loses because 2:34's negated-existence clause explicitly reopens his case as its own move after that unit's own summary closure at 2:33 had already shut the tally.

boundary_rationale: The row opens on וּבְנֵ֤י כָלֵב֙ אֲחִ֣י יְרַחְמְאֵ֔ל (v.42; WEB 'The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel were Mesha his firstborn ... and the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron'), and holds together a run of place-founding descendants. Two further verses inside this stretch do open with the identical waw+venei+PN shape used at 2:42 itself, and each needs its own disposition rather than a blanket denial that either exists. וּבְנֵ֖י חֶבְר֑וֹן (v.43, 'The sons of Hebron') continues rather than restarts the line, since Hebron is the figure v.42's own closing clause has just named (מָרֵשָׁ֖ה אֲבִ֥י חֶבְרֽוֹן, 'Mareshah the father of Hebron'); v.43 unpacks him at once, the same immediate-unpacking move this chapter uses elsewhere (e.g. 2:9-10's Hezron-to-Ram). וּבְנֵ֖י יָהְדָּ֑י (v.47, 'The sons of Jahdai') is a harder case: Jahdai has no antecedent anywhere in this register — the name occurs nowhere else in the book — so its attachment to the Caleb material rests on list-position alone rather than on any stated filiation, and this is the row's genuinely weakest join rather than a non-issue. Subsequent generations (2:44-45) run through Shema, Rekem, and Shammai's own line without renaming Caleb, and two concubines' notices (2:46, 2:48) do keep Caleb himself as the standing subject — 'standing subject' fits those two verses specifically, not the whole 2:43-47 stretch — ending on Caleb's own daughter, וּבַת כָּלֵ֖ב עַכְסָֽה (v.49; WEB '...and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah.'). The unit closes at 2:50 because that verse reopens with a full summary that re-heads Caleb under a third designation, אֵ֤לֶּה הָיוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י כָלֵ֔ב בֶּן ח֖וּר בְּכ֣וֹר אֶפְרָ֑תָה (v.50; WEB 'These were the sons of Caleb, the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah:') — a verse-initial elleh-hayu heading with its list following, the same opening shape used at 3:1 (וְאֵ֤לֶּה הָיוּ֙, also elleh-hayu) but not at 2:1, whose own opening lacks hayu entirely (אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י, with no hayu at all); the seam rests on that heading itself, not on any place-founder contrast with 2:42-49, since that stretch already runs its own series of avi-X toponym-founder constructions (2:42 twice, 2:44, 2:45, 2:49 three times, seven in all) and so cannot be distinguished from 2:50-55 on that ground. 'Son of Hur' is not a clean third label independent of this chapter's own text: 2:19-20 make Hur Caleb's own son (וַתֵּ֥לֶד ל֖וֹ אֶת חֽוּר, v.19; וְחוּר֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת, v.20), so the designation is a text-internal genealogical crux rather than settled proof the chapter keeps two Caleb strands formally apart; the seam rests on the verse-initial heading and the subject-matter turn, not on the uniqueness of 'son of Hur' as a label. A samekh follows 2:46 inside this row and another falls at its very close, 2:49 (single-witness), the latter corroborating the seam the re-head at 2:50 already makes on its own.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this row with the following 2:50-55 unit into one continuous Caleb register loses because 2:50 opens with the verse-initial elleh-hayu heading this chapter otherwise reserves for fresh openings (2:1, 3:1) and pivots to place-founder material absent from 2:42-49, not because 'son of Hur' is a uniquely third label — that designation is itself complicated by 2:19-20 making Hur Caleb's own son; splitting 2:47 (Jahdai) out as its own row is the harder rival this row concedes rather than defeats, since Jahdai has no antecedent anywhere in the register and the row keeps him inside 2:42-49 on list-position alone.

boundary_rationale: The row opens on the re-head just discussed, אֵ֤לֶּה הָיוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י כָלֵ֔ב בֶּן ח֖וּר בְּכ֣וֹר אֶפְרָ֑תָה (oshb:1Chr.2.50; WEB 'These were the sons of Caleb, the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal the father of Kiriath Jearim'), and runs through town-founder sons (2:50-51), Shobal's own descendants and the Kiriath Jearim clans (2:52-53), to Salma's settlements (2:54), closing on the Kenite scribal coda, הֵ֚מָּה הַקִּינִ֣ים הַבָּאִ֔ים מֵחַמַּ֖ת אֲבִ֥י בֵית רֵכָֽב (oshb:1Chr.2.55; WEB 'These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.'). That coda is grammatically continuous with 2:54's settlement list (its 'these' points back to the scribal families just named at Jabez, not to a fresh subject), so it stays attached rather than standing alone. The whole Judah/Caleb complex ends decisively at 2:55 because 3:1 opens an unmistakably different register — David's own house — with וְאֵ֤לֶּה הָיוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י דָויִ֔ד (oshb:1Chr.3.1; WEB 'Now these were the sons of David'), matching the block division the campaign strategy draws between the Judah/Caleb cycles and David's house. A samekh follows 2:53 inside this row, and a second falls at the row's very close, 2:55 (single-witness), corroborating both the chapter's end and the section break expected here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching 2:55's Kenite coda as its own decision loses because it is grammatically continuous with 2:54's settlement list via the resumptive 'these', not marked off by any fresh register head of its own.

boundary_rationale: The register head opens the chapter and the David's-house block together, וְאֵ֤לֶּה הָיוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י דָויִ֔ד אֲשֶׁ֥ר נֽוֹלַד ל֖וֹ בְּחֶבְר֑וֹן (v.1; WEB 'Now these were the sons of David, who were born to him in Hebron:'), and runs through the six Hebron-born sons named by birth order (3:1-3), a regnal notice giving Hebron and Jerusalem reign-lengths, וַיִּ֨מְלָךְ שָׁ֔ם שֶׁ֥בַע שָׁנִ֖ים וְשִׁשָּׁ֣ה חֳדָשִׁ֑ים (v.4; WEB '...and he reigned there seven years and six months...'), and the Jerusalem-born sons (3:5-8) -- introduced by their own waw-plus-elleh formula, וְאֵ֥לֶּה נוּלְּדוּ ל֖וֹ בִּירוּשָׁלָ֑יִם (v.5; WEB 'and these were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon, four, by Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel;'), reproducing v.1's own opening device (the waw-prefixed elleh, a passive n-l-d verb, the dative lo, and a locative), a recurrence rare enough in chs.2-4 that it could be mistaken for a fresh register head; it stays inside this row's still-open 'sons of David' frame rather than opening a rival one because it names no new register subject, only a further set of sons born to the same David v.1's own head already governs, before closing on an explicit summary, כֹּ֖ל בְּנֵ֣י דָוִ֑יד מִלְּבַ֥ד בְּֽנֵי פִֽילַגְשִׁ֖ים וְתָמָ֥ר אֲחוֹתָֽם (v.9; WEB 'All these were the sons of David, in addition to the sons of the concubines; and Tamar was their sister.'). That closure is a kol-summary, not a bare numeral tally: the span's actual bare-numeral tallies stand at אַרְבָּעָ֔ה (v.5, 'four') and תִּשְׁעָֽה (end of v.8, 'nine'), ; v.5's four sits mid-verse with the roster continuing on through v.8, but v.8's nine is a sub-total that ends the Jerusalem-born list itself -- nothing follows it but v.9's own summary -- without yet closing the row, which still needs v.9's kol-plus-exception clause to do that; so it is the kol-plus-exception-clause shape of v.9, not the presence of a number as such, that marks the row's own end. The regnal notice sits inside the still-open head rather than closing it, since more of David's own sons follow immediately, not a new subject. The unit ends firmly at 3:9 because 3:10 opens a different form altogether, the plain succession chain וּבֶן שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה רְחַבְעָ֑ם (v.10; WEB 'Solomon's son was Rehoboam'), naming one heir per generation rather than summarizing all of a king's sons. A pe follows 3:9 (single-witness); it carries the same tier-3 weak-corroboration weight as any samekh cite in this book, per the Writings marker policy, and is not ranked above the samekh that falls after 3:4, which sits at the internal Hebron/Jerusalem hinge this row does not split on.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at 3:4's regnal notice loses because the notice sits inside the still-open 'sons of David' head, and the unit is not closed until the explicit kol-summary of 3:9.

boundary_rationale: This row opens on the succession-chain form וּבֶן שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה רְחַבְעָ֑ם אֲבִיָּ֥ה בְנ֛וֹ (v.10; WEB 'Solomon's son was Rehoboam, Abijah his son'), which names one heir per generation with the bare 'his son' refrain, no verb and no head, straight through to אָמ֥וֹן בְּנ֖וֹ יֹאשִׁיָּ֥הוּ בְנֽוֹ (v.14; WEB 'Amon his son, and Josiah his son.'). The plural construct head that opens the next three verses is the same shape each time: וּבְנֵי֙ יֹאשִׁיָּ֔הוּ (v.15, 'The sons of Josiah'), וּבְנֵ֖י יְהוֹיָקִ֑ים (v.16, 'The sons of Jehoiakim'), and וּבְנֵי֙ יְכָנְיָ֣ה (v.17, 'The sons of Jeconiah') all open with the identical construction, so the head-form boundary actually falls between v.14 and v.15, not later; the row's own genealogical material for vv.15-16 does not repeat the singular-heir idiom of vv.10-14 but continues the plural head-form that also opens v.17, one verse past this row's own close. v.16 itself names two sons under that plural head, not one: וּבְנֵ֖י יְהוֹיָקִ֑ים יְכָנְיָ֥ה בְנ֖וֹ צִדְקִיָּ֥ה בְנֽוֹ (v.16; WEB 'The sons of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, and Zedekiah his son.'), so vv.15-16 form a two-verse plural-head unit rather than a fold back into the single-heir chain. That plural-head shift nonetheless keeps vv.15-16 attached to the chain that precedes it rather than opening a fresh row: Josiah's and Jehoiakim's sons continue the same uninterrupted, still-royal Davidic succession in strict regnal sequence, with no change of era, so the shift from singular 'his son' to plural 'sons of' reads as a counting device inside one still-continuous line, not as a seam. What actually distinguishes v.17 from vv.15-16, given that all three share the same opening construction, is the epithet that follows it: וּבְנֵי֙ יְכָנְיָ֣ה אַסִּ֔ר (v.17; WEB 'The sons of Jeconiah, the captive:'), 'the captive,' which has no counterpart at v.15 or v.16 and reframes the line as post-exilic. That epithet, אַסִּ֔ר, is anarthrous and occupies the same syntactic slot personal names occupy immediately after it -- שְׁאַלְתִּיאֵ֖ל בְּנֽוֹ follows it directly in the same verse, and 3:18 continues with six more bare names -- so the appellative 'the captive' reading is witness-supported (WEB so renders it) but not formally compelled by the Hebrew alone; the seam's strength rests in part on that translational choice rather than on the Hebrew morphology by itself. No pe or samekh falls anywhere between 3:10 and 3:16 in this list, so this boundary, like the last row's, rests on wording alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at 3:15, where the plural head-form first displaces the singular succession chain, is the harder rival this row must concede ground to rather than dismiss: vv.15-17 do share one head-form across a boundary this row draws through the middle of it. The row nonetheless holds 3:10-16 together because the epithet at v.17 ('the captive') is the only feature in vv.10-17 that marks a content-level break -- a post-exilic reframing -- while the head-form shift at v.15 marks only a change from singular to plural counting within the still-royal, still-pre-exilic line.

boundary_rationale: The unit opens on the captivity-marked head וּבְנֵי֙ יְכָנְיָ֣ה אַסִּ֔ר שְׁאַלְתִּיאֵ֖ל בְּנֽוֹ (v.17; WEB 'The sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son,'), which the preceding row's chain never uses — no earlier king in 3:10-16 carries an epithet of this kind — so the exile itself functions as the tier-1 opening marker here. From there the register runs appositionally through Pedaiah, Zerubbabel, Hananiah, Shecaniah, Neariah, and Elioenai's own sons (3:18-23) without a further 'sons of X' restart strong enough to split it, down to the row's own close. 3:21 alone carries five further ben/benei-X heads in a single verse, וּבֶן חֲנַנְיָ֖ה פְּלַטְיָ֣ה וִישַֽׁעְיָ֑ה בְּנֵ֤י רְפָיָה֙ בְּנֵ֣י אַרְנָ֔ן בְּנֵ֥י עֹבַדְיָ֖ה בְּנֵ֥י שְׁכַנְיָֽה (v.21), yet the cluster reads as one bare lineal descent chain rather than four further candidate register restarts, since each 'sons of' link is a single-word patronymic (Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah, Shecaniah) with no independent development of its own before the next link picks it up, the same appositional pattern already argued for 3:19. That close names seven sons of Elioenai, but the quotation must disclose a ketiv/qere pair rather than run both forms together as if they were separate names: וּבְנֵ֣י אֶלְיוֹעֵינַ֗י (v.24, 'the sons of Elioenai') is followed by the unpointed ketiv and its pointed qere as one name, הדיוהו הוֹדַוְיָ֡הוּ, then וְאֶלְיָשִׁ֡יב וּפְלָיָ֡ה וְ֠עַקּוּב וְיוֹחָנָ֧ן וּדְלָיָ֛ה וַעֲנָ֖נִי (Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani), closing on שִׁבְעָֽה ('seven'). Read literally without that disclosure the line displays eight name-tokens against its own stated count; resolved on the qere alone, the arithmetic is exact at seven, and it is this exactness -- not a shared formula with any other closure in the book -- that argues 3:24 ends something. The parallel drawn earlier in this campaign to 2:4 and 2:6 does not hold and is withdrawn: those verses close with a kol/kulam word plus a numeral, while 3:24 closes on the bare numeral alone, and that same bare-numeral shape recurs three further times inside this very row without closing anything -- חָמֵֽשׁ at v.20, שִׁשָּֽׁה at v.22, שְׁלֹשָֽׁה at v.23 -- so a device the span itself repeats four times cannot be what marks its own end; only the seven-count's internal exactness, once the ketiv/qere is resolved, does that work. The row's actual closing edge is argued from the next verse's own wording: 4:1 opens asyndetically with the tribal head בְּנֵ֖י יְהוּדָ֑ה (WEB 'The sons of Judah'), no conjunctive waw, against every verse from 4:2 through 4:20 opening with one -- a genuine tier-1 restart at the tribal level, one register above anything inside 3:17-24, rather than an appeal to any part-tiling boundary external to the text. Samekh marks stand at 3:21 and at the row's own close, 3:24 (single-witness); neither is weighed as a driver, only as silent tier-3 agreement.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at 3:19, where Zerubbabel's own sons are listed, loses not because no new register head reopens there -- 3:19 in fact carries two, וּבְנֵ֣י פְדָיָ֔ה זְרֻבָּבֶ֖ל וְשִׁמְעִ֑י at the verse's own opening and a second, וּבֶן זְרֻבָּבֶל֙, later in the same verse -- but because each head names a figure the immediately preceding clause has just introduced: Pedaiah from 3:18, Zerubbabel from 3:19a itself, Hananiah from 3:19b, Shecaniah from 3:21, Neariah from 3:22, and Elioenai from 3:23. No head in the run introduces an unannounced subject, so the whole post-captivity line from Jeconiah through Elioenai's seven sons remains one register.

boundary_rationale: Opens the part at the tribal-level register head בְּנֵ֖י יְהוּדָ֑ה (v.1; WEB 'The sons of Judah'), a bare list-head naming five sons with no verb, matching the register-head device used to launch supplementary Judahite material after ch.3's royal line. The unit then tracks Hur's own branch through two nested sub-closures before its own final one: v.2 traces Shobal's son Reaiah two generations down to Ahumai and Lahad, closing on a family-level formula, אֵ֖לֶּה מִשְׁפְּח֥וֹת הַצָּֽרְעָתִֽי (v.2; WEB 'These are the families of the Zorathites'); v.3 opens a further branch, וְאֵ֨לֶּה֙ אֲבִ֣י עֵיטָ֔ם (v.3; WEB 'These were the sons of the father of Etam'), naming Etam's three sons and their sister. Both are sub-branch closures nested inside the larger register, not row-ending summaries in their own right: v.2's formula closes only the Zorathite families' local material, and v.3's own list runs on to v.4 with no closure of its own until v.4's own formula retroactively claims the broader scope, אֵ֤לֶּה בְנֵי חוּר֙ בְּכ֣וֹר אֶפְרָ֔תָה אֲבִ֖י בֵּ֥ית לָֽחֶם (v.4; WEB 'These are the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, the father of Bethlehem') -- 'the sons of Hur' names the same figure v.1 lists as one of Judah's five sons, so v.4's closure is the one that reaches back over the whole vv.2-4 stretch, gathering Reaiah's and Etam's branches together under Hur rather than ending at either sub-closure along the way. That gathering is not stated within ch.4 itself -- v.1 lists Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal as five co-ordinate sons of Judah with no filiation given between Hur and Shobal there -- but rests on 2:50's own testimony that Shobal, Reaiah's father, descends from Hur (אֵ֤לֶּה הָיוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י כָלֵ֔ב בֶּן ח֖וּר בְּכ֣וֹר אֶפְרָ֑תָה שׁוֹבָ֕ל אֲבִ֖י קִרְיַ֥ת יְעָרִֽים, 'these were the sons of Caleb, the son of Hur... Shobal'), which supplies the link 4:4's closure alone does not make explicit. The close is confirmed by the next verse's shift to a dative-fronted new subject, וּלְאַשְׁחוּר֙ אֲבִ֣י תְק֔וֹעַ הָי֖וּ שְׁתֵּ֣י נָשִׁ֑ים (v.5; WEB 'Ashhur the father of Tekoa had two wives'), which introduces an unrelated Hezron branch rather than continuing Hur's line.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v.2 or v.3, where each carries its own interior 'these are' formula, loses because both are branch-level closures that v.4's own closure re-gathers under Hur's name, and extending the row through 4:8 to include Ashhur's two wives loses because that steps past v.4's summary and v.5's new-subject opening without warrant.

boundary_rationale: Opens with the frame-setting notice וּלְאַשְׁחוּר֙ אֲבִ֣י תְק֔וֹעַ הָי֖וּ שְׁתֵּ֣י נָשִׁ֑ים חֶלְאָ֖ה וְנַעֲרָֽה (v.5; WEB 'Ashhur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah'), which governs the whole unit: Naarah's own sons are born by a wayyiqtol verb, וַתֵּ֨לֶד ל֤וֹ נַעֲרָה֙ (v.6; 'Naarah bore him'), and close internally at the same verse with אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י נַעֲרָֽה (v.6; WEB 'These were the sons of Naarah'). Helah's branch then follows at v.7, naming her sons and stopping there -- וּבְנֵ֖י חֶלְאָ֑ה צֶ֥רֶת יצחר וְצֹ֖חַר וְאֶתְנָֽן (v.7; WEB 'The sons of Helah were Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan') -- -- disclosing the unpointed ketiv יצחר and its pointed qere וְצֹ֖חַר as one name, matching the ketiv/qere disclosure decision M8-1Chr-020 already gives at 3:24, so the three printed name-tokens match the three sons WEB and this row both report -- with no ben or avi particle connecting the fresh clause that opens v.8, וְק֣וֹץ הוֹלִ֔יד אֶת עָנ֖וּב וְאֶת הַצֹּבֵבָ֑ה וּמִשְׁפְּח֥וֹת אֲחַרְחֵ֖ל בֶּן הָרֽוּם (v.8; WEB 'Hakkoz became the father of Anub, Zobebah, and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum'), back to Helah, Naarah, or Ashhur; Hakkoz's own attachment to this row rests on his position in the sequence rather than on any stated filiation, and that inference is flagged here rather than asserted as textual fact. Wayyiqtol as such does not mark the row's own end, since v.6 already opens with one inside this span; what actually sets v.9 apart is not its conjugation but its content -- a named human subject carrying an evaluative predicate and a direct-speech frame, וַיְהִ֣י יַעְבֵּ֔ץ נִכְבָּ֖ד מֵאֶחָ֑יו (v.9; WEB 'Jabez was more honorable than his brothers'), a form no verse in vv.5-8 shares.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding Hakkoz's unclosed line together with Jabez into one row treats v.8's silence as an invitation to keep going, but it ignores that v.9 introduces a named, evaluated human subject with a direct-speech frame that nothing in vv.5-8 shares, a content-level break wayyiqtol alone cannot mark since v.6 already uses the same conjugation inside this span.

boundary_rationale: The inset opens on a named individual with a wayyiqtol clause, "וַיְהִ֣י יַעְבֵּ֔ץ נִכְבָּ֖ד מֵאֶחָ֑יו" (WEB "Jabez was more honorable than his brothers"), then runs a direct-speech petition into a resolution clause, "וַיָּבֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֵ֥ת אֲשֶׁר שָׁאָֽל" (WEB "God granted him that which he requested"). That petition-and-fulfillment shape has no counterpart anywhere else in the surrounding fragments, which are pure toledot chains. The close is confirmed by v.11's explicit return to that chain-form, "וּכְל֥וּב אֲחִֽי שׁוּחָ֖ה הוֹלִ֣יד" (WEB "Chelub the brother of Shuhah became the father of Mehir"), which resumes the host register's own idiom rather than continuing Jabez's story.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The book strategy's default is that a register-framed inset stays inside its host row; applied here that would merge 4:5-11 into one row treating Jabez as a third branch off Hakkoz. That merger is the strongest rival, but it has to explain away the wayyiqtol entry at v.9 and the toledot-chain resumption at v.11, both of which are tier-1 form breaks the merger reading cannot account for.

boundary_rationale: Resumes the host register's toledot idiom at וּכְל֥וּב אֲחִֽי שׁוּחָ֖ה הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת מְחִ֑יר (v.11; WEB 'Chelub the brother of Shuhah became the father of Mehir'), which carries no benei/ben head at all, and runs a string of family fragments -- some plural-headed, e.g. וּבְנֵ֣י קְנַ֔ז (v.13, 'The sons of Kenaz'), and one singular-headed, וּבֶן עֶזְרָ֔ה (v.17, 'The sons of Ezrah') -- against the plural heads at vv.13,15,16,19,20 -- none of which carries a tribal-level head naming Judah or Simeon directly, the level this cluster's other rows split on. Two of these fragments do close with the chapter's own summary device, and both are named here rather than passed over: v.12 ends its verse on אֵ֖לֶּה אַנְשֵׁ֥י רֵכָֽה (WEB 'These are the men of Recah'), while v.18's own elleh-clause, וְאֵ֗לֶּה בְּנֵי֙ בִּתְיָ֣ה בַת פַּרְעֹ֔ה (WEB 'These are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh'), is followed in the same verse by the relative clause אֲשֶׁ֥ר לָקַ֖ח מָֽרֶד ('whom Mered took') rather than closing the verse outright -- a difference from 4:12 that if anything strengthens the row's point, since v.18's summary caps its family fragment inline and folds straight back into the sentence rather than standing as a verse-final formula. Both instances use the same elleh-summary device that closes v.6's fragment in the neighboring row (אֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֥י נַעֲרָֽה, 'These were the sons of Naarah') without forcing a split there either, though not an identical formula: 4:12 substitutes anshei for benei and closes on a place-name rather than a person, and 4:18 is waw-prefixed while 4:6 is not. In each case the closure caps one name's line before the run continues to the next fragment on the same conjunctive footing, rather than closing a register the way the tribal-level closures elsewhere in this book do. The run ends where the pattern actually breaks: v.21 opens with the bare, vav-less head בְּנֵי֙ שֵׁלָ֣ה בֶן יְהוּדָ֔ה (WEB 'The sons of Shelah the son of Judah'), an asyndetic restart that reprises Judah's name directly, unlike any verse since v.1. Single-witness marks fall at 4:12 (SAMEKH), 4:14 (PE), and 4:18 (SAMEKH), disclosed here as tier-3 corroboration of the family-fragment breaks already argued from the wording, never as what drives the row's own outer edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this stretch into a separate row at each conjunctive head (Chelub, Kenaz, Caleb, Jehallelel, Ezrah, Hodiah's wife, Shimon) would be the finer-grained rival, but no one of those seven openings carries a tribal-level head the way Judah's or Simeon's own headings do elsewhere in this book -- not their shared conjunctive form, which in fact varies between plural and singular -- so subdividing at one over another has no tier-1 basis.

boundary_rationale: Opens with the asyndetic head "בְּנֵי֙ שֵׁלָ֣ה בֶן יְהוּדָ֔ה" (WEB "The sons of Shelah the son of Judah"), which -- unlike every intervening conjunctive fragment since v.11 -- explicitly restates Judah's name, marking a fresh sub-tribal register on Judah's third son. It runs through a craftsmen guild note that closes with the source-note remark "וְהַדְּבָרִ֖ים עַתִּיקִֽים" (WEB "These records are ancient"), then a settlement notice, "הֵ֚מָּה הַיּ֣וֹצְרִ֔ים ... יָ֥שְׁבוּ שָֽׁם" (WEB "These were the potters ... they lived there with the king for his work"), which supplies the row's own closure (SAMEKH follows, oshb:1Chr.4.23, single-witness) before Simeon's tribal head opens at 4:24.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading v.21 as one more unheaded fragment continuing row 4 loses because it has to ignore that v.21 alone, among vv.11-23, drops the conjunctive vav and repeats Judah's own name -- the same register-head shape used at v.1.

boundary_rationale: Opens the Simeon block at the tribal-level head בְּנֵ֖י שִׁמְע֑וֹן (v.24; WEB 'The sons of Simeon'), but v.24 itself is not a chain: it lists five sons side by side with no beno ('his son') link anywhere in the verse, נְמוּאֵ֣ל וְיָמִ֔ין יָרִ֖יב זֶ֥רַח שָׁאֽוּל (Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, Shaul). The father-son chain proper only begins at v.25, שַׁלֻּ֥ם בְּנ֛וֹ מִבְשָׂ֥ם בְּנ֖וֹ מִשְׁמָ֥ע בְּנֽוֹ (Shallum his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son), and runs one further verse before it is itself interrupted: v.26 reopens with a plural construct head, וּבְנֵ֖י מִשְׁמָ֑ע (v.26; WEB 'The sons of Mishma'), a conjunctive, vav-prefixed benei-X shape that recurs further into the book at 5:1, 5:11, and 5:23 -- distinct from the asyndetic, vav-less benei heads at 4:21 and at this row's own opening, 4:24 itself. That formal difference between the row's own asyndetic head and 4:26's conjunctive one supports, rather than weakens, keeping 4:26 unit-internal: a genuinely fresh register-opening head in this row's own idiom would be asyndetic like 4:24, not conjunctive like 4:26. Here the same head stays unit-internal rather than opening a fresh row because it re-heads a figure the chain has just named one clause earlier (Mishma, v.25's third link) purely to continue his own line — חַמּוּאֵ֥ל בְּנ֛וֹ זַכּ֥וּר בְּנ֖וֹ שִׁמְעִ֥י בְנֽוֹ (Hammuel his son, Zaccur his son, Shimei his son) — rather than to introduce an unrelated branch the way the sibling rows' own tribal-level heads do; the register is a tribal head (v.24) plus a segmented five-way list (v.24) plus a beno-chain that is itself re-headed once, at the same figure the chain was already tracking, rather than a branch-free single-file descent line throughout. The row closes on a comparative remark rather than a lineage note, עַד בְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה (v.27; WEB '... didn't multiply like the children of Judah'; SAMEKH follows, single-witness), which brings the descent-chain to a rhetorical stop before the verb-form shifts to settlement narration at v.28.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 4:24-38 as one Simeon row (matching the coarser book-level block map) is the strongest rival, but it passes over v.28's distinct wayyiqtol settlement-formula opener without argument; the segmented-list-plus-chain register and the settlement register are different forms even though both concern Simeon.

boundary_rationale: Opens with the settlement formula וַיֵּֽשְׁב֛וּ בִּבְאֵֽר שֶׁ֥בַע (v.28; WEB 'They lived at Beersheba'), listing cities held until David's reign and closing that inner list at אֵ֥לֶּה עָרֵיהֶ֖ם עַד מְלֹ֥ךְ דָּוִֽיד (v.31; WEB 'These were their cities until David's reign'), then extending to the surrounding villages, which close in turn at זֹ֚את מוֹשְׁבֹתָ֔ם וְהִתְיַחְשָׂ֖ם לָהֶֽם (v.33; WEB 'These were their settlements, and they kept their genealogy'). That second closure is not a row-ending summary but a promissory one: it announces that a genealogical enrollment ('and they kept their genealogy') was kept for these settlements, and the material that follows without any new register head, a named roster of family princes running from v.34 to v.38, is that enrollment made explicit -- v.33's own wording forward-points to exactly what v.34-38 supplies. That reading has an in-book precedent for the enrolment root (yod-het-sin) functioning as an opener rather than a closer: at 5:7, בְּהִתְיַחֵ֖שׂ ('when the genealogy was reckoned') introduces, rather than seals, the names running on into 5:8. The pattern is not uniform, and the campaign discloses the fuller distribution rather than the favorable case alone: a full sweep of the hitpael of this root across the book returns exactly ten verses (4:33, 5:1, 5:7, 5:17, 7:5, 7:7, 7:9, 7:40, 9:1, 9:22), and most of the other nine function as terminal, roster-closing instances (5:17, 7:5, 7:9, 7:40, 9:1; 7:7 counts a clan sub-total) -- the counter-pattern this row's own reading of 4:33 runs against. Six of the ten are followed by a pe or samekh (5:17, 7:5, 7:7, 7:9, 7:40, 9:1); the other four, including this row's own 4:33 and the opener at 5:7, carry no mark at all -- mark-absence is shared by 5:1, 5:7, and 9:22 as well, so it is not distinctive to 4:33 and offers no independent corroboration either way. The row's own closing formula, אֵ֚לֶּה הַבָּאִ֣ים בְּשֵׁמ֔וֹת נְשִׂיאִ֖ים בְּמִשְׁפְּחוֹתָ֑ם וּבֵית֙ אֲב֣וֹתֵיהֶ֔ם פָּרְצ֖וּ לָרֽוֹב (v.38; WEB 'these mentioned by name were princes in their families ... increased greatly'), accordingly closes the whole compound unit v.33 opened toward, not merely the roster alone. The seam to v.39 is nonetheless real, though not because the material there is unrelated to this row's own close: v.39's wayyiqtol scene-shift, וַיֵּלְכוּ֙ לִמְב֣וֹא גְדֹ֔ר (v.39), opens a narrative episode whose own participants are later identified by back-reference to exactly the roster this row closes on, וַיָּבֹ֡אוּ אֵלֶּה֩ הַכְּתוּבִ֨ים בְּשֵׁמ֜וֹת (v.41, 'these written by name came'), echoing v.38's own elleh ... beshemot. That anaphora makes the roster the narrative's grammatical antecedent, not its content; the register (a named list, participle-headed) and the raid narrative (a wayyiqtol scene with named actions and a place) remain formally distinct devices even where the second supplies its subject from the first, the same register-supplies-narrative-subject relation this book uses elsewhere between a roster and an inset built on it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v.33, where the settlement material closes with its own 'these were their settlements' formula, is the strongest rival -- place-register 28-33 capped at 33, name-roster 34-38 capped at 38 -- but it loses because v.33's own closing clause explicitly promises the genealogical record ('they kept their genealogy') that v.34-38 then supplies with no fresh head of its own, making v.33 a transitional closure within one compound unit rather than the row's actual end.

boundary_rationale: Opens the Simeon coda with the wayyiqtol scene-shift וַיֵּלְכוּ֙ לִמְב֣וֹא גְדֹ֔ר (v.39; WEB 'They went to the entrance of Gedor'), a bare 3mp verb with no expressed subject in either v.39 or the verb that opens v.40; the first explicit subject in the span is itself a back-reference at v.41, וַיָּבֹ֡אוּ אֵלֶּה֩ הַכְּתוּבִ֨ים בְּשֵׁמ֜וֹת (v.41, 'these written by name came'), pointing to the roster the preceding row closes on at 4:38. That dependency does not pull 4:34-38 into this row: the roster supplies the coda's grammatical subject without the coda continuing the roster's own form, a participle-headed name list, into this span's wayyiqtol narrative, and the two remain the register/narrative-inset pairing this book uses elsewhere. Concretely: at 5:18-19, the muster roster's own list supplies the subject for the subjectless 3mp verb that opens the war narrative, וַיַּעֲשׂ֥וּ ('and they made war'); and at 5:23-24/5:25, the roster of Manasseh's heads supplies the subject for the subjectless 3mp apostasy verb, וַיִּֽמְעֲל֔וּ ('and they trespassed'). The episode narrates a Hezekiah-era pasture expedition and Meunim conquest, closing not on a verse-final refrain but verse-medially: עַד הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה (v.41, 'to this day') stands at a genuine clause boundary of its own -- its הַזֶּ֔ה carries a zaqef qatan (disjunctive) -- but is followed in the same verse by וַיֵּשְׁב֖וּ תַּחְתֵּיהֶ֑ם כִּֽי מִרְעֶ֥ה לְצֹאנָ֖ם שָֽׁם ('and lived in their place, because there was pasture there for their flocks'), so the episode's actual close is a pasture-and-flock notice, not the day-formula. That notice completes an inclusio with the episode's own opening motive, לְבַקֵּ֥שׁ מִרְעֶ֖ה לְצֹאנָֽם (v.39, 'to seek pasture for their flocks') answered by כִּֽי מִרְעֶ֥ה לְצֹאנָ֖ם שָֽׁם (v.41) — the same pasture-for-flocks phrase framing episode one more exactly than the day-formula does. A second episode opens at וּמֵהֶ֣ם מִן בְּנֵ֣י שִׁמְע֗וֹן הָלְכוּ֙ (v.42; WEB 'Some of them, even of the sons of Simeon ... went') and closes verse-finally on עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה (v.43, 'to this day'); this occurrence, unlike v.41's, is also verse-final: its הַזֶּֽה carries the verse-end pointing that closes the verse outright. What binds the two episodes into one coda is not a matched, identical refrain — the two occurrences of 'to this day' carry different cantillation and only the second sits at a verse's own end — but the continuous Simeonite subject and the shared conquest-then-settlement pattern each episode runs in turn.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the Gedor pasture-conquest (39-41) from the Seir Amalekite raid (42-43) as two rows is the strongest rival, since each names a different destination and captain-list and only the second episode's day-formula is genuinely clause-final; it loses because both episodes share one continuous Simeonite subject and run the identical conquest-then-settlement pattern in turn, a structural link the day-formula alone does not have to carry.

boundary_rationale: Opens the Transjordan block at “וּבְנֵ֨י רְאוּבֵ֥ן בְּכֽוֹר יִשְׂרָאֵל֮ כִּ֣י ה֣וּא הַבְּכוֹר֒ וּֽבְחַלְּלוֹ֙ יְצוּעֵ֣י אָבִ֔יו נִתְּנָה֙ בְּכֹ֣רָת֔וֹ לִבְנֵ֥י יוֹסֵ֖ף בֶּן יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְלֹ֥א לְהִתְיַחֵ֖שׂ לַבְּכֹרָֽה” (WEB “The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father’s couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel; and the genealogy is not to be listed according to the birthright.”), which is immediately interrupted by a parenthetical on the forfeited birthright (5:1b-2); a weak SAMEKH stands at that aside's own close (oshb:1Chr.5.2, single-witness) -- exactly the seam a reader might use to peel the aside off as its own unit -- but under the Writings policy this tier-3 mark is weak corroboration only and cannot drive that split against the tier-1 signal that follows. The register then relaunches itself, its head phrase recurring consonantally -- repointed for its new clause-initial position, and without the conjunctive vav -- “בְּנֵ֥י רְאוּבֵ֖ן בְּכ֣וֹר יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל חֲנ֥וֹךְ וּפַלּ֖וּא חֶצְר֥וֹן וְכַרְמִֽי” (WEB “the sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.”), before running the Joel-Beerah line (5:4-6) and the Bela settlement note. 5:4 opens with its own verse-initial asyndetic construct head, “בְּנֵ֖י יוֹאֵ֑ל שְׁמַֽעְיָ֥ה בְנ֛וֹ גּ֥וֹג בְּנ֖וֹ שִׁמְעִ֥י בְנֽוֹ” (WEB “The sons of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son,”) -- Joel is not among the four sons 5:3 has just named -- but unlike 5:3's verbatim relaunch of 5:1's own phrase, 5:4 carries no such repetition tie; it is a clan-internal sub-head introducing one further lineage inside the still-open Reuben register, this comparandum to 4:26 is withdrawn, since 4:26 re-heads a figure (Mishma) the chain had named one clause earlier, while Joel here has no such antecedent at 5:3. What keeps 5:4 inside the still-open Reuben register instead is that Joel is picked up again as an ancestor later within this same register, at 5:8's own genealogy (שֶׁ֖מַע בֶּן יוֹאֵ֑ל, 'Shema the son of Joel'), so the sub-head opens material the register itself later reclaims rather than introducing a wholly unrelated branch. It closes on the Saul-era Hagrite notice, “וּבִימֵ֣י שָׁא֗וּל עָשׂ֤וּ מִלְחָמָה֙ עִם הַֽהַגְרִאִ֔ים וַֽיִּפְּל֖וּ בְּיָדָ֑ם וַיֵּשְׁבוּ֙ בְּאָ֣הֳלֵיהֶ֔ם עַֽל כָּל פְּנֵ֖י מִזְרָ֥ח לַגִּלְעָֽד” (WEB “In the days of Saul, they made war with the Hagrites, who fell by their hand; and they lived in their tents throughout all the land east of Gilead.”; PE follows, oshb:1Chr.5.10, single-witness), before Gad's own tribal head opens at 5:11.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Peeling the birthright aside (5:1b-2) off into its own row against the genealogy proper (5:3-10) is the strongest rival -- weakly seconded by the SAMEKH at 5:2 -- but the aside is only a dependent clause, never capped by any summary-type formula, and v.3's verbatim repetition of v.1's head phrase reads as a relaunch of the same unit, not the opening of a new one; 5:4's own asyndetic head is a weaker second rival still, since it lacks that repetition tie and instead functions as a clan-internal sub-head like this cluster's other internal 'sons of X' pivots.

boundary_rationale: Opens with the tribal head “וּבְנֵי גָ֣ד לְנֶגְדָּ֗ם יָֽשְׁב֛וּ בְּאֶ֥רֶץ הַבָּשָׁ֖ן עַד סַלְכָֽה” (WEB “The sons of Gad lived beside them in the land of Bashan to Salecah:”), runs chiefs and genealogy (5:12-15), a samekh follows 5:13 (single-witness), sitting exactly at the internal join between the Gad chiefs (5:12-13) and the Abihail lineage (5:14-15); as tier-3 evidence it weakly corroborates an internal seam there but is outweighed by the register's own unbroken run to the dated closure at 5:17, then a settlement notice sharing its opening verb with decision 027's own opening formula -- “וַיֵּֽשְׁב֛וּ בַּגִּלְעָ֥ד בַּבָּשָׁ֖ן וּבִבְנֹתֶ֑יהָ וּבְכָֽל מִגְרְשֵׁ֥י שָׁר֖וֹן עַל תּוֹצְאוֹתָֽם” (WEB “They lived in Gilead in Bashan and in its towns, and in all the pasture lands of Sharon as far as their borders.”), whose first word is the identical fully-accented form 4:28 uses to open that earlier row -- but here the notice stays internal, subordinated to the dated closure one verse later rather than functioning as a fresh register head, since nothing marks a break between 5:15's genealogy and 5:16's settlement report. The row closes on that dated formula naming two kings, “כֻּלָּם֙ הִתְיַחְשׂ֔וּ בִּימֵ֖י יוֹתָ֣ם מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה וּבִימֵ֖י יָרָבְעָ֥ם מֶֽלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל” (WEB “All these were listed by genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel.”; PE follows, oshb:1Chr.5.17, single-witness). The next verse abandons the single-tribe head for a combined muster of three groups, “בְּנֵֽי רְאוּבֵ֨ן וְגָדִ֜י וַחֲצִ֥י שֵֽׁבֶט מְנַשֶּׁה֮ מִן בְּנֵי חַיִל֒ אֲ֠נָשִׁים נֹשְׂאֵ֨י מָגֵ֤ן וְחֶ֨רֶב֙ וְדֹ֣רְכֵי קֶ֔שֶׁת וּלְמוּדֵ֖י מִלְחָמָ֑ה אַרְבָּעִ֨ים וְאַרְבָּעָ֥ה אֶ֛לֶף וּשְׁבַע מֵא֥וֹת וְשִׁשִּׁ֖ים יֹצְאֵ֥י צָבָֽא”, marking the row's outer edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading v.18's muster as Gad's own continuation (since Gad is named again there) is the strongest rival, but v.18 explicitly renames all three Transjordan groups under one numbered census formula, a form distinct from the single-tribe head and dated closure that frame 5:11-17.

boundary_rationale: Opens on a joint-tribe census formula naming all three Transjordan groups together, “בְּנֵֽי רְאוּבֵ֨ן וְגָדִ֜י וַחֲצִ֥י שֵֽׁבֶט מְנַשֶּׁה֮ מִן בְּנֵי חַיִל֒ אֲ֠נָשִׁים נֹשְׂאֵ֨י מָגֵ֤ן וְחֶ֨רֶב֙ וְדֹ֣רְכֵי קֶ֔שֶׁת וּלְמוּדֵ֖י מִלְחָמָ֑ה אַרְבָּעִ֨ים וְאַרְבָּעָ֥ה אֶ֛לֶף וּשְׁבַע מֵא֥וֹת וְשִׁשִּׁ֖ים יֹצְאֵ֥י צָבָֽא” (WEB “The sons of Reuben, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, of valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword, able to shoot with bow, and skillful in war, were forty-four thousand seven hundred sixty that were able to go out to war.”), a numbered-muster form that has no counterpart in the single-tribe heads of 5:1-17. The war narrative that follows closes with an exile-flagged formula, “כִּֽי חֲלָלִ֤ים רַבִּים֙ נָפָ֔לוּ כִּ֥י מֵהָאֱלֹהִ֖ים הַמִּלְחָמָ֑ה וַיֵּשְׁב֥וּ תַחְתֵּיהֶ֖ם עַד הַגֹּלָֽה” (WEB “For many fell slain, because the war was of God. They lived in their place until the captivity.”; PE follows, oshb:1Chr.5.22, single-witness), after which v.23 reopens a single-tribe head for half-Manasseh alone. The strongest case for reading the war and the final deportation as one continuous unit rests on the root-play below; 5:22's closing עַד הַגֹּלָֽה ("until the captivity") shares its root with 5:26's וַיַּגְלֵם֙ ("and he exiled them"), a root-play that points forward from this war unit's own close to the Transjordan complex's close four verses later. Yet the two are still kept apart: v.23's single-tribe head for half-Manasseh, its own separate genealogy, and its own apostasy notice (5:25) intervene and resolve this war unit first, before that later exile is narrated; the root-play anticipates the complex's ultimate outcome without erasing the intervening register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 5:18-26 as one row spanning both the war and the final joint deportation is the strongest rival -- sharpened by the root-play between 5:22's עד הגלה and 5:26's ויגלם, which points forward from this unit's own close toward that later exile -- but v.23's intervening single-tribe head for half-Manasseh and its own separate apostasy notice (5:25) already resolve this war unit before that later register begins.

boundary_rationale: Opens with the single-tribe head “וּבְנֵ֗י חֲצִי֙ שֵׁ֣בֶט מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה יָשְׁב֖וּ בָּאָ֑רֶץ מִבָּשָׁ֞ן עַד בַּ֧עַל חֶרְמ֛וֹן וּשְׂנִ֥יר וְהַר חֶרְמ֖וֹן הֵ֥מָּה רָבֽוּ” (WEB “The children of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They increased from Bashan to Baal Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon.”), runs a heads-of-households roster, then pivots on the apostasy wayyiqtol “וַיִּֽמְעֲל֔וּ בֵּאלֹהֵ֖י אֲבוֹתֵיהֶ֑ם וַיִּזְנ֗וּ אַחֲרֵי֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י עַמֵּי הָאָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁר הִשְׁמִ֥יד אֱלֹהִ֖ים מִפְּנֵיהֶֽם” (WEB “They trespassed against the God of their fathers, and played the prostitute after the gods of the peoples of the land whom God destroyed before them.”), whose verbs are 3mpl with the Transjordan tribes as subject. That chain continues unbroken into the deportation clause naming all three Transjordan groups collectively, “וַיָּעַר֩ אֱלֹהֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל אֶת ר֣וּחַ פּ֣וּל מֶֽלֶךְ אַשּׁ֗וּר וְאֶת ר֨וּחַ֙ תִּלְּגַ֤ת פִּלְנֶ֨סֶר֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר וַיַּגְלֵם֙ לָראוּבֵנִ֣י וְלַגָּדִ֔י וְלַחֲצִ֖י שֵׁ֣בֶט מְנַשֶּׁ֑ה וַ֠יְבִיאֵם לַחְלַ֨ח וְחָב֤וֹר וְהָרָא֙ וּנְהַ֣ר גּוֹזָ֔ן עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה” (WEB “So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgath Pilneser king of Assyria, and he carried away the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and brought them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and to the river of Gozan, to this day.”; PE follows, oshb:1Chr.5.26, single-witness) -- but the grammatical subject shifts at this join: 5:26 opens with its own explicit 3ms nominal subject, the God of Israel, and its own verbs (וַיַּגְלֵם֙ 'and he exiled them,' וַ֠יְבִיאֵם 'and he brought them') carry the tribes only as object suffixes, not as subject. The wayyiqtol sequence itself is unbroken -- it is v.25's direct narrative consequence -- even though the acting subject changes from the tribes to God as the agent of the punishment; that shift is what makes the verse a single sin-and-consequence unit rather than two, closing the row and the whole Transjordan complex on the refrain “עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה” ("to this day"). Immediately after, MT 5:27 (= WEB 6:1) opens offset zone A with the Levi register head, בְּנֵ֖י לֵוִ֑י גֵּרְשׁ֕וֹן קְהָ֖ת וּמְרָרִֽי, confirmed by the documented Gershon/Gershom spelling anchor against MT 6:1's בְּנֵ֖י לֵוִ֑י גֵּרְשֹׁ֕ם קְהָ֖ת וּמְרָרִֽי, marking the true outer boundary of this row and of the Transjordan complex as a whole.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Pulling v.26 free as its own book-level closing notice, separate from Manasseh's register in 5:23-25, is the strongest rival, but v.26 continues the same wayyiqtol chain begun at v.25 as its direct narrative consequence -- the acting subject shifts from the tribes to God, but the chain itself does not break -- so it cannot be detached from the apostasy notice it resolves.

boundary_rationale: Opens at 6:1 with the book's base register formula, “The sons of Levi” over בְּנֵ֖י לֵוִ֑י (oshb 1Chr.5.27), naming the three clans; this row sits inside dual-cite zone A, and 6:1's spelling of Gershon, גֵּרְשׁ֕וֹן, is the anchor form the offset crosswalk turns on (contrast the Gershom spelling that opens the next block at web:1Chr.6.16). The cascade narrows twice more by the identical device: 6:2 “The sons of Kohath” over וּבְנֵ֖י קְהָ֑ת (oshb 5.28), then 6:3a “The children of Amram” over וּבְנֵ֣י עַמְרָ֔ם (oshb 5.29, double samekh, single-witness — disclosed per the doubling), which itself opens into “the sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.” It closes at 6:3b/4a: the moment the text pivots from bare name-lists to the fathering formula “Eleazar became the father of Phinehas” (oshb 5.30) marks the seam, since none of 6:1-3's three heads predicate anything of their members, while 6:4 begins a run that predicates a father-son act at every link.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row through 6:15 would lose the tier-1 form-shift at 5:30 from bare son-lists to the toledot-style fathering chain that structures the rest of the high-priestly line.

boundary_rationale: Opens where the previous row closes: 6:4's “Eleazar became the father of Phinehas” renders the fathering-verb chain (oshb 5:30) that then carries father to son through twenty-one further links -- Phinehas, Abishua, Bukki, Uzzi, Zerahiah, Meraioth, Amariah, Ahitub, Zadok, Ahimaaz, Azariah, Johanan, a second Azariah, a second Amariah-Ahitub-Zadok sequence, Shallum, Hilkiah, a third Azariah, Seraiah, and Jehozadak -- without a fresh register head interrupting it anywhere, unlike the three separate “sons of X” heads that opened decision 033. One link breaks the hiphil-perfect fronted-subject form the rest of the chain uses: web:1Chr.6.11 = oshb:1Chr.5.37 opens with the wayyiqtol וַיּ֥וֹלֶד עֲזַרְיָ֖ה, verb before subject, immediately after the 6:10 aside (oshb 5:36) -- but referential continuity carries across that join regardless (the same Azariah is understood as both the aside's subject and the begetter here), and no register-head formula of any kind interrupts the chain at that point or anywhere else in the span, so the unit's integrity rests on that absence rather than on verbal uniformity. A single explanatory aside at 6:10 (“who executed the priest's office in the house that Solomon built,” oshb 5:36) names an office without breaking the chain's grammar, so it stays inside. The unit closes at 6:15 (= oshb 5:41), where the final link, Jehozadak, does not become father of anyone; the clause instead narrates his own fate, “וִיהוֹצָדָ֣ק הָלַ֔ךְ בְּהַגְל֣וֹת יְהוָ֔ה אֶת יְהוּדָ֖ה וִירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם בְּיַ֖ד נְבֻכַדְנֶאצַּֽר” (WEB “Jehozadak went into captivity when Yahweh carried Judah and Jerusalem away by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.”; weak samekh, single-witness) -- an exile notice that halts the succession list rather than extending it, paralleling the book's other exile-closure at 5:25-5:26 (no offset). 6:16 (= oshb 6:1) then restarts the whole “sons of Levi” head under the Gershom spelling, confirming the seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off 6:10's priestly-office notice as its own row would isolate a single explanatory aside that carries no register or narrative frame of its own.

boundary_rationale: 6:16 reopens the “sons of Levi” head that decision 034's chain had closed, but spelled Gershom, גֵּרְשֹׁ֕ם (oshb 6:1), against 5:27's Gershon, גֵּרְשׁ֕וֹן (oshb 5:27) -- the very spelling pair the offset crosswalk verifies. Two further heads follow at the same shared sibling generation as this triad itself (not decision 033's three-generation Levi-Kohath-Amram descent, a different depth entirely): 6:17 opens with an elleh-shemot naming formula, distinct from a bare construct head, “וְאֵ֛לֶּה שְׁמ֥וֹת בְּֽנֵי גֵרְשׁ֖וֹם לִבְנִ֥י וְשִׁמְעִֽי” (WEB “These are the names of the sons of Gershom: Libni and Shimei.”), naming Libni and Shimei as its own enumerated content; 6:18 “the sons of Kohath were…” (וּבְנֵ֖י קְהָ֑ת עַמְרָ֣ם וְיִצְהָ֔ר וְחֶבְר֖וֹן וְעֻזִּיאֵֽל) and 6:19a “the sons of Merari…” (בְּנֵ֥י מְרָרִ֖י מַחְלִ֣י וּמֻשִׁ֑י) continue as bare construct heads at that same sibling level. The unit closes at 6:19b with a toledot-style summary absent from decision 034's cascade: “these are the families of the Levites according to their fathers' households,” over וְאֵ֛לֶּה מִשְׁפְּח֥וֹת הַלֵּוִ֖י לַאֲבוֹתֵיהֶֽם -- a sealing formula that closes on the absence of any further enumeration following it, unlike 6:17's elleh, which opens directly onto the two names it introduces; nothing of this closural shape recurs again before the settlement-total colophon at oshb:1Chr.6.45 (= web:1Chr.6.60), and its own final word, לַאֲבוֹתֵיהֶֽם, is a genuine hapax occurring nowhere else in the book, sharper evidence of its sealing force than the bare presence of elleh, which itself recurs doing the same closural work at oshb 4:2 (no offset). This formula hands off to the patrilineal expansion 6:20 opens with a resumptive “Of Gershom” rather than a fourth “sons of X” head.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 16-19 into the expansion that follows would erase the closural force of 6:19b's 'families…fathers' households' formula -- sealed by a word that is a hapax in this book and by the absence of any enumeration following it, unlike 6:17's own elleh -- which has no counterpart inside the ensuing chains.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:1Chr.4.2 = oshb:1Chr.4.2 (MT, no offset, samekh, single-witness)

boundary_rationale: Opens at 6:20 where the formula shifts from decision 035's “sons of X” heads to a resumptive prefixed patronymic, “Of Gershom” over לְֽגֵרְשׁ֑וֹם (oshb 6:5), followed by a “his son” succession chain -- the same head-to-chain shift that opened decision 034, now recurring at the clan level rather than the priestly-line level. The chain runs Gershom's line (20-21), then re-picks up Kohath's name at 6:22, בְּנֵ֖י קְהָ֑ת עַמִּינָדָ֣ב בְּנ֔וֹ קֹ֥רַח בְּנ֖וֹ אַסִּ֥יר בְּנֽוֹ (oshb 6:7), and Merari's at 6:29, בְּנֵ֥י מְרָרִ֖י מַחְלִ֑י לִבְנִ֥י בְנ֛וֹ שִׁמְעִ֥י בְנ֖וֹ עֻזָּ֥ה בְנֽוֹ (oshb 6:14) -- both waw-less construct 'sons of X' forms, morphologically identical to the heads decisions 033 and 035 treat as row-constituting.
